name: Goryeo
summary: The Korean kingdom that gave Korea its English name. It is famous for celadon pottery, the Tripitaka Koreana woodblocks and early metal movable type.

location.value: The Korean peninsula, ruled from Gaegyeong (Kaesong).

terrain.value: Mountains, rivers and coasts of the Korean peninsula.

climate.value: Temperate, with cold winters and monsoon summers.

resources.value: Rice, ginseng, timber and fine clay for celadon pottery.

disasters.value: No specific disasters are recorded beyond droughts and floods in the chronicles.

population.source: Wikipedia: Goryeo (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

urbanisation.value: Gaegyeong had about 70 temples in the 11th century.

migration.value: Refugees from Balhae after its fall (926).

economicBase.value: Rice farming on state and aristocratic land.

tradeRoutes.value: Trade with Song China; Arab merchants also came.
tradeRoutes.source: Wikipedia: Goryeo (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: Goryeo coins, though trade often used cloth and rice.
moneyAndTax.source: Wikipedia: Goryeo (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

inequality.value: Aristocratic clans and Buddhist temples held much land; many people were slaves.

governmentType.value: Monarchy; a military regime held power from 1170 to 1270.
governmentType.source: Wikipedia: Goryeo (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

succession.value: Hereditary in the royal Wang family.

institutions.value: Civil service exams (from 958) and Tang-style ministries.

stability.value: Military officers held real power from 1170 to 1270.

eliteConflict.value: Civil versus military officials, leading to the military coup of 1170.

armyAndTech.value: Infantry and fortress defence; the Sambyeolcho units resisted the Mongols.

territoryChange.value: Became a vassal (son-in-law state) of the Mongol Yuan (1270–1356).
territoryChange.source: Wikipedia: Goryeo (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: the Khitan Liao, Jurchen Jin and Mongols; friendly with Song China.

inventions.value: Printing with metal movable type; the Jikji (1377) is the oldest surviving such book.

scienceEducation.value: Civil service exams and Confucian academies; the national academy (Gukjagam, 992).

openness.value: Open to trade with Song China and Arab merchants.

communicationTransport.value: Post stations along roads; sea trade with Song China from the port of Byeongnando.

religion.source: Wikipedia: Goryeo (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

languageWriting.value: Korean, with Classical Chinese for writing.
languageWriting.source: Wikipedia: Goryeo (checked 6 Nov 2026); Seth, A History of Korea (2010)

artsArchitecture.value: Celadon pottery, Buddhist painting and the Tripitaka Koreana.

sharedIdentity.value: Claimed to be the successor of the ancient kingdom of Goguryeo (hence the name).

dailyLife.value: Tiled houses for nobles, thatched for farmers, with ondol floor heating; rice, vegetables and tea.

neighbours.value: Song China, the Khitan Liao, the Jurchen Jin, the Mongols, and Japan.

ideasReligions.value: Buddhism and Neo-Confucianism came from China; Neo-Confucianism shaped the later Joseon.

riseSignals.value: Taejo reunified the Later Three Kingdoms by 936.

peakPeriod.value: The 11th century, after the victory over the Khitan, a golden age of Buddhist culture.

declineSignals.value: Military rule, Mongol invasions, then Red Turban and Japanese pirate raids in the 14th century.

outcome.value: General Yi Sŏng-gye took power in a coup; he founded Joseon in 1392.

sources.value: The Goryeosa (History of Goryeo, 15th century). Checked against Wikipedia (“Goryeo”).

overallCertainty.value: Good for politics; some dates (Tripitaka editions) differ between sources.

knownFor.label: Goryeo celadon
knownFor.note: Jade-green glazed pottery, often with inlaid designs.

knownFor.label: Tripitaka Koreana
knownFor.note: Over 80,000 carved woodblocks of Buddhist scriptures, kept at Haeinsa.

knownFor.label: Metal movable type
knownFor.note: The Jikji (1377) is the oldest surviving book printed with metal type.
